In you all deaths gather, all the broken glasses, the sere pages, the derangements of thought, they gather in you, guilty of all deaths, incomplete and guilty, in the wake of every mother, in your wake, motionless. They gather there, in your weak hands. The apples of this market are death, these poems retreat into their grammar, in the hotel room, in the hut of what does not join, souls without rest, aged lips, bark ripped from the trunk. They are dead. They gather there. They failed, the operation failed, they failed. The place was motionless, the word obscure. That was the place we agreed on. Goodbye, memory of the sparkling nights, goodbye, big smile, the place was there. To breathe was a darkness shutters had made, a primitive state. Silence and desert were switching positions and we were talking to a lamp. The place was that one. The trolleys rarely passed. Venus was returning to her hut. Out of the warrior throat, episodes broke free. We didn't say anything more. The place was that one. It was there that you were dying.

outputs.L4:
The sky is a bruised throat, frozen mid-swallow. 

Here, at the center of the salt-bleached expanse, stands the spire. It does not lean; it does not rise. It simply sits, heavy and calcified, against a horizon that swallowed its sun long ago. No wind visits this place. The dust lies where it fell a century past, a grey sheet over a bed that will never again be unmade.

In the courtyard of the spire, the endeavors lie scattered. 

Brass telescopes, their lenses cracked like spiderwebs, point blind eyes toward a ceiling of iron clouds. Blueprints, once inked with the arrogant geometry of human ambition, have rotted into fragile lace. A grand engine sits half-assembled, its iron teeth seized by rust, locked in a silent bite against time itself. We carved our names into the foundations. We built ladders of glass. We swore the light would return if we only climbed high enough.

The glass broke. The rungs surrendered. 

Inside the spire’s shadow, memory bleaches away. A hand reaches into the gloom, but the fingers are made of chalk, crumbling at the knuckles. What was the name of the river? What was the shape of the mouth that once whispered in the dark? First, the colors vanish—the red of the copper, the blue of the summer sky—leaving only shades of ash. Then the sounds dissolve. The ocean becomes a faint ringing in the ears; the ringing becomes a hum; the hum becomes a hollow, aching void. 

A pulse staggers in the quiet. Slow. Thick. A dying swimmer treading water in a sea of lead. 

The floor tilts. The motionless setting begins its slow, vertical retreat. It is not the world falling away, but the mind slipping off the ledge of being. The architecture collapses inward—not with a roar, but with a breathless sigh. The maps burn without fire. The rusted gears turn to dust. Every song ever sung, every tower ever built, every sorrow ever wept fades into the same grey neutrality.

The light pinches down to a single, shivering thread. 

Then, a snap. 

The thread severs. Darkness floods the chamber, heavy as wet stone, filling the mouth, the eyes, the empty spaces where ambition once burned. 

There is no echo. There is no aftermath. The shadows swallow even themselves, settling into an absolute, unyielding stillness. The silence is not a pause between breaths; it is the final, heavy curtain. The quiet is complete. The darkness is total. 

Nothing remains to remember that anything ever was.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an avant-garde prose poem inspired by Samuel Beckett and French surrealism, focusing on themes of grief, failed connection, and the weight of memory.
counterfactuals.output:
The room has five corners today. One for you, one for me, three for the dead. We sit on the edge of the iron bedstead, waiting for the ceiling to lower its eyelids. 

Say something. Anything. A syllable to crack the plaster. 

Instead, you open your mouth and a small, dry moth flutters out, landing softly on the rim of my empty saucer. We watch it die of drought. This is our third conversation this century. Or perhaps it is the first, repeated until the grammar dissolves into grease. 

Memory is an overcoat made of wet gravel. I try to take it off, but the buttons are sewn into my collarbones. Underneath, the ribs are full of old bus tickets and your name, spelled backward, smelling of formaldehyde. Do you remember the sea? No, it was not the sea. It was a zinc bucket filled with dark oil, and we drowned a clock in it to make the afternoon stay. The afternoon stayed. It is still staying. It has rotted into the floorboards.

I reach for your hand across the small distance—three inches, four light-years, a chasm of unwashed linen. My fingers pass straight through your wrist. You are made of smoke and salt tonight. Or maybe I am the one made of tin. We collide like two empty coats hanging in a drafty hallway. *Tink. Tink.* A sound like a spoon striking a tooth.

"Finish," you whisper, though your lips are painted on a piece of cardboard leaning against the wardrobe. 

"Finished," I reply to the skirting board. "It is nearly finished. All the light has run out of the knees."

We wait. The silence grows a thick, grey fur. It climbs up our ankles, up to our waists. We cannot move. We must move. The door has been painted over so many times it is now just part of the wall’s internal bleeding. Tomorrow we will attempt the window, but the window only opens inward, into a museum of our own abandoned shoes. 

Nothing to be done. The grief is a heavy piano trapped in the throat. I play a single key. It makes no sound, but a black bird drops from the ceiling and lands perfectly in my palm, cold as a coin, twice as heavy. I offer it to you. You bite your tongue to keep from swallowing the rain. 

We sit. We go on sitting. The room contracts by an inch. The gravel in the coat shifts.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a melancholic, fragmented prose poem about finality and death.
counterfactuals.output:
The light retreats first. A slow, violet hemorrhage against the baseboards. The clock doesn't count down anymore; it merely counts out. One less. One less. 

A hand left on the counter, palm up. An abandoned shell. We were talking about rain, I think. Or the way cedar smells when it burns. Now, only the ash. The cold, soft weight of it.

There is no grand falling of curtains. Only a latch slipping into place. A thread pulled until the cloth simply ceases to be cloth. 

The tea cools. Dust settles on the sill, indifferent to the quiet. A name forgotten mid-syllable. *Shhh.* The water has stopped humming in the pipes.

Finality is not a storm. It is the absolute absence of echo. 

The last breath—a dry leaf scraped across slate. Then, the slate itself forgets the sound. Nothing comes after the period. Just the blank white of the page, holding its breath forever.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in paragraph form that includes surreal imagery of broken glasses, a hotel room, talking to a lamp, and Venus, with the repeating phrase "The place was that one."
counterfactuals.output:
The wallpaper bled faded damask into the shadows, and **the place was that one**. On the stained carpet of Room 409, a pair of reading glasses lay crushed beneath the weight of an invisible foot, their spiderwebbed lenses multiplying the dresser into a thousand fractured cathedrals of dust. I walked across the floor, but my feet trod on the reflection of the ceiling, where upside-down rain leaked upward into the pale plaster. Each shard of broken glass held a tiny, humming universe of static, catching the distant, violet pulse of the hallway light leaking beneath the door. **The place was that one**, where the room key was carved from solid salt and dissolved the moment I tried to lock out the night.

I pulled up a chair of woven wire and leaned my cheek against the warm brass of the bedside lamp, conversing softly with its yellow filament. "Where do the lost hours go?" I whispered, and the lamp hummed its burning, silent answer in a dialect of scorched moths and forgotten telephone calls, its silk shade tilting like an attentive ear listening for a heartbeat in the drywall. It flickered in three long pulses—a secret code written in heat—and ignited the air with the scent of ozone and crushed carnations. **The place was that one**. Through the grimy windowpane, the planet Venus burned like an unblinking eye of acid and gold, descending through a plum-colored sky until it hovered just past the fire escape, so close its brilliance began to melt the wire frames on the rug.

Venus poured its sweltering, ancient radiance through the blinds, casting stripes of liquid bronze across the bed until the fractured lenses began to mend themselves into tiny, slithering mirrors that crept across the floorboards. I told the lamp my true name, and it blazed so brightly the hotel room turned inside out, spilling its velvet furniture into the vast, suffocating clouds of the morning star. The walls fell away like dry ash, leaving only the bed, the talking bulb, and the shattered spectacles reflecting a sky that rained molten copper. **The place was that one**, where every light bulb harbored a goddess, every shadow bled into space, and the dawn arrived wrapped in broken glass.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Explore the concept of a desolate place where all brokenness, obscure memories, and incomplete deaths gather, written in a dreamlike, literary stream-of-consciousness style.
counterfactuals.output:
It begins at the hem of a coat that was never mended, right where the thread frayed and gave up wanting to hold. You fall into it sideways—or perhaps you were always sitting here, ankle-deep in the gray salt, watching the horizon curl up like the edges of a burnt letter. 

There are no corners here, only soft, wet intersections of fog that smell of old pine needles and iron. The air is thick with static, the kind that lives between radio stations at three in the morning when the heart is too loud and the room is too cold. Listen. It’s not wind. It’s the murmur of every forgotten telephone number, every face you loved before you learned the shape of your own eyes, dissolving into the soil. 

Look down. The ground is made of shards, but they don't cut. Here is the teacup with its handle broken off, still holding the temperature of a Tuesday from thirty years ago; beside it lies the promise someone made while holding their breath under a yellow streetlamp, yellow like sulfur, yellow like a bruise that refused to bloom. And the memories—oh, they don't linger like pictures, they linger like damp wool. You touch a patch of air and suddenly your mouth tastes of copper and the swing set you fell from when you were six, except the swing set is made of your father’s voice when he was tired, and the ground is an ocean of unread mail.

And the half-dead things. They are the quietest. 

They sit in the hollows where the light forgets to reach, neither corpse nor ghost, just the long, unspooled ribbons of things that refused to finish dying. A moth with half a wing, fluttering in the rhythm of a failing pacemaker. A love affair that didn't end, just starved to death in a locked drawer, its ribs visible beneath transparent skin. The men who came back from the fire but left their names in the smoke—they drift like tallow candles, blinking, waiting for an exhale that never comes. They are the incomplete deaths, the ones that got stuck between the click of the latch and the opening of the door. They breathe, but the breath is only secondhand winter.

A bell rings, but it has no clapper. The sound is just the *idea* of a chime, floating past a mountain of abandoned shoes. One shoe is red. It belonged to a girl who stopped walking halfway across a bridge, not because she jumped, but because she simply ceased to move forward, and the rest of her life went on without her like an empty train. 

You pick up a piece of glass. In it, you see a room you’ve never been in, but you know the curtains. You know the way the dust settles on the windowsill at four o’clock. You remember the smell of the rain on the screen, but you don't know who you were when you smelled it. Was it you? Or was it the person you were supposed to be before the gears slipped?

Everything here is waiting, but there is no time to wait *for*. The sky is the color of a wet slate, heavy with rain that will never fall because the clouds have forgotten how to condense. A clock ticks, but it has only one hand, and it sweeps relentlessly over a face of pure white chalk, rubbing itself out, erasing the seconds as it claims them. 

*Hush.* 

A shadow crosses your feet. It isn't yours. It's the shadow of a dream you had when you were feverish, the one about the house with too many stairs, bleeding into the shadow of an old dog that died behind the shed while everyone was asleep. They curl together like dry leaves in the rain. 

You try to speak, but your voice comes out as sea foam, white and cold and full of tiny, breaking bubbles, each one holding a sentence that died in a throat: *I’m sorry, I meant to, I thought we had, please don't—*

They float away into the gray. They join the silt. The ground settles. Another inch of ash. Another unremembered name. The tide comes in, but it isn't water; it’s just the slow, heavy rising of everything that was ever left undone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
